preheader: Apple shipped a drag-and-drop designer for Wallet passes; an Idiocracy parody site arguing the word AI is now illegal topped Hacker News; Germany released a 78-billion-parameter sovereign model on Unity Day and a Berlin engineer took its tokenizer apart; India goes into Monday on an eighth straight losing week; and 8.02 lakh units of donated blood expired in India last year because the clock on them is shorter than the queue.

quote.text: If at first the idea is not absurd, then there is no hope for it.
quote.author: Albert Einstein
quote.note: Most of us use plausibility as a filter: if an idea sounds sensible, pursue it. Einstein is pointing out that this filter has already been run by everybody else, so whatever passes it is either done or crowded. The useful inversion is that the feeling of absurdity is not a warning, it is a coordinate — it tells you nobody has looked here yet.

items.text: Stop reviewing the diff and make Claude review you instead: "Grill me on these changes and don't make a PR until I pass your test." It flips who is accountable for understanding the code, and it surfaces the three lines you were about to approve without reading.
items.source: Anthropic's Claude Code team, in the official power-user tips

hn.title: Apple Pass Designer
bullets: Apple has shipped a macOS app that builds Apple Wallet passes without writing any code. You start from an Apple-supplied or custom template, drop in a logo, background and strip image from whatever design tool you already use, set background, foreground and label colours, and fill the standard fields for the pass type — boarding passes, event tickets, store cards and generic passes.

The preview is the selling point. It updates as you type and shows the pass as it will look on both iPhone and Apple Watch, which is the part that normally costs you a build-sign-install cycle per tweak.

The interesting feature is semantic tags. Adding structured data — event dates, venue locations, flight details — is what makes Siri Suggestions, Calendar entries and Maps directions light up off a pass. The app writes those tags for you, and separately generates a non-semantic version of the same pass for older systems, so you can view the two side by side.
It also validates as you go, flagging missing required values and definitions it did not expect. That is the error class that otherwise shows up as a pass that silently fails to install.

Practical limits: it is a beta, it needs macOS 27 or later, and it wants you signed in with an Apple Account under the Developer Agreement — free to register. Documentation sits at developer.apple.com under walletpasses, "Creating a pass with Pass Designer".

hn.title: Extra Big Ass Intelligence
bullets: It is a single-page Idiocracy parody with no byline, built as a fake government product page. The masthead reads "EXTRA BIG ASS INTELLIGENCE™ — Federally Mandated Super Intelligence (SI)", the subtitle is "SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) v1.0 — AI.exe has been deleted by decree", and the scrolling ticker promises "PURE UNLEADED SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) BY EXECUTIVE ORDER ★ NO REFUNDS, NO APOLOGIES, NO 'AI' — THAT WORD IS ILLEGAL NOW".

The whole joke is the two-letter rebrand. One of the fake news tiles reads "Congress Discovers One Weird Trick To Fix The Economy", with the subhead "(IT'S A TWO-LETTER REBRAND)". Another is "Local 35B Parameter Model Wants To Chat In Your Area", subhead "(ZERO REFUSAL VECTORS)". A third offers subsidised dopamine injections for your depressed AI, "side effects include optimism".

There is a working chat box of "pre-approved stupidity chips" — canned prompts including "Why will 'Super Intelligence' save the economy?" and "Why do plants crave Brawndo?" — under the line "warning: every chip lowers its opinion of you". Counters at the bottom track "TERAFLOPS WASTED TODAY" and "GALLONS OF BRAWNDO CONSUMED".

The sharpest bit is a mock interstitial: "WENDY'S DYNAMIC MENU™ — Algorithmic Caloric Ingestion. SURGE PRICING DETECTED: This burger is now $24.50 based on local demand, your pupil dilation, and your declining credit score." The accept button's small print says that by glancing at the ad you agreed to download the app and surrendered your biometric location data in perpetuity.

The comment thread spent most of its energy on a second-order joke: that the page's gradient bubbles, emoji section headers and unnecessary Tailwind build make it look like it was itself generated by a model. One commenter suggested that was the watermark. The footer disclaims responsibility for "physical harm, loss of ego, or existential dread".

hn.title: Kolibri: A Sovereign Open-Weight Model
bullets: Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on 3 October — German Unity Day, which is not an accident — under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face. It is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active per token: 50 layers, 384 experts each plus one shared expert, six experts routed per forward pass.

The attention design is what buys the context window. Sliding-window attention over 512 tokens on most layers, with full attention every fifth layer, which gets it to 1M tokens without additional positional tricks.

The training mix is the whole pitch. 20 trillion pre-training tokens at 62% English, 21.3% German and 14% code, with roughly 4.3T German tokens assembled from curated Common Crawl (1.3T), rephrasing (1T) and open datasets, through a bilingual English-German tokenizer with a 128,000 vocabulary. Pre-training took 21 days on 768 B200 GPUs at 16k sequence length, followed by mid-training on 3.44T tokens at 64k and long-context adaptation on 200B at 256k.
Published numbers: AIME 2025 at 96.9 in English and 87.5 in German, AIME 2026 at 96.0 and 90.0, GPQA Diamond 84.3 and 81.3, HumanEval+ 92.7, and Humanity's Last Exam 21.5 in English, 15.9 in German.

The target customer is named explicitly — public administration, aerospace, manufacturing — and the company's framing of sovereignty "combines two dimensions: how we built the model, and how it transfers to our customers". The release is positioned as continuous iteration from the earlier Kolibri Origin rather than a new line.

hn.title: Newgrounds.com – A community of games, music, and art
bullets: The front page carries a 1995-2026 copyright line and a site-wide Spooktober theme, and the thing that makes it worth a visit is that the architecture never changed. Forums, a portal, user subdomains, a daily top-list bot. The scale behind it: 1,170,388 topics and 19,889,182 posts, with 3,810 registered users online when we looked.

The Game Development board still carries its own history in its description — "Formerly the Flash forum. All other devs now welcome!" — and it is the biggest room in the building at 182,624 topics and 1,598,524 posts. Flash has been dead for years; the forum that was built around it is the busiest part of the site.

What is actually being discussed is ordinary and specific, not nostalgic. The hot threads right now are "Halloween Spooktacular 2026!" (14,607 views, 99 replies), "October 2026 Art General", "CALLING VOICE ACTORS (Need VAs)", "evil bit tricks" in the programming forum, and a 32,568-view standing PSA about portfolio threads.

Two live controversies are visible from the board index alone. "Age Verification after end of Supporter Upgrade?" has 3,996 views and 50 replies in the help forum, and the animation board's top thread is "Tommy Boy is likely playing 4D chess to protect Oney" at 2,133 views and 84 replies — the moderation row the HN thread kept circling back to.

Featured on the front page when we checked: Out of the Nest (2,594 views), Grunt Clicker, a "Madness themed sandbox clicker", and Nonogravs, made during Falling Blocks Jam 2026. Still a staff list of twenty-three named moderators, still a link to buy a T-shirt.

hn.title: Aleph Alpha Kolibri: How the sovereign German LLM works
bullets: Tejas Kumar, an AI engineer at IBM in Berlin, read the 189-page technical report on the day of release and wrote the version with the numbers that matter. He also ran one experiment himself, on the tokenizer, which turns out to be where the model's advantage actually lives.

His test: the German Federal Constitution costs Kolibri's UniBPE tokenizer 35,190 tokens against GPT-5's 41,482 — 17.9% fewer. On the compound "Bundesverfassungsgericht", GPT-5 spends six tokens and Kolibri two. Across German text generally he measures 11.2% fewer tokens, which is a discount on every German prompt you will ever send it.

The anti-hallucination work is trained in, not prompted. Four reasoning levels (none, low, medium, high) and roughly 800,000 German reasoning examples trained with a "Merlin-Arthur protocol" — a three-player game in which the model learns to admit it does not know. On Artificial Analysis's Omniscience test it refuses or partially answers 44% of the time when it lacks the knowledge, against 11.1% for Qwen3.5 35B-A3B.

He is equally clear about where it is bad, which the launch post is not. Closed-book retrieval 51.0, last of twelve models compared. Multi-turn tool calling 39.8. Terminal-Bench 2.1 coding 27.7. And mid-range context is worse than long context: 67.9 at 128,000 tokens against Qwen3.5's 89.9, even though Kolibri scores 63.2 on RULER at a full million.

The deployment catch, in his words: it "computes like a 3.5 billion parameter model but needs the memory of a 78 billion parameter one" — about 78GB, so two A100s or H100s minimum, or one H200/B200/B300. His verdict is a bank, a public authority or an aerospace supplier running German documents on-premises; he is using it for neurological patient assessment in Berlin hospitals. It is, he says, "the wrong pick for a coding agent".

stories.headline: Nothing has happened to Indian equities since Thursday, and that is the problem going into Monday
stories.source: Goodreturns' week-ahead outlook published Saturday 3 October, with HDFC Sky's close report for the Thursday 1 October session, NiftyTrader's FII/DII cash data for 1 October, Bajaj Broking's trade setup for 5 October, and PTI via Deccan Herald on the rupee. Next Indian session: Monday 5 October.
bullets: There was no Indian session on Friday — the NSE and BSE were shut for Mahatma Gandhi Jayanti — and none over the weekend, so Thursday 1 October is still the last print. Sensex 71,909.70, down 570.59 points or 0.79%; Nifty 50 22,421.95, down 198.50 points or 0.88%. Anything quoting an Indian index move for 2, 3 or 4 October is quoting nothing.

That close ended an eighth consecutive losing week, the longest such run in 25 years: Nifty down 3.1% on the week, Sensex down 2.7%, and 8.7% and 8.4% respectively across the eight. On Thursday itself 2,916 stocks fell against 1,306 that rose, Nifty Midcap lost 1.1%, and Nifty IT was the one sector up — 2.2% on the day, 0.5% on the week — on Infosys at ₹1,035 (+4.11%) and TCS at ₹2,075 (+1.19%). Autos were the wreck: Bajaj Auto ₹10,045, down 7.62%, Maruti Suzuki ₹11,386, down 4.86%.

Flows tell the same story twice. On 1 October FIIs sold ₹9,484 crore of cash equities and DIIs bought ₹10,042 crore, a net plus of ₹558 crore — domestic money absorbing all of it and a little more. Over the week FIIs sold ₹34,966 crore, a seventh straight week of net selling, against DII buying of ₹33,455 crore.

The causes are all imported and none of them resolved over the weekend. Brent back above $100, the US 10-year at 5.34% on Thursday — its highest since 2002 — and the rupee at 96.31, down 37 paise on the day and at a more-than-two-month low. India buys its oil in dollars; those three numbers are one number.

What Monday is set up around: Nifty support at 22,250 then 22,000, resistance at 22,700, with Bank Nifty's zone 54,000-53,500 against 55,000-55,100. India VIX closed at 14.5 and the daily RSI at 22.5, which is oversold enough that a bounce would not mean anything. The RBI's rate-setting committee meets Monday to Wednesday with the decision on 7 October, and the repo rate has been at 5.25% for four reviews running.

trends.headline: Your telco has been hiding the cheap recharges, and from now on they go in the first tab
trends.subject: TRAI directs Jio, Airtel, Vodafone Idea and BSNL to create a dedicated 'TRAI-Mandated Packs' section as the first tab on prepaid recharge screens in apps, websites and exclusive retail outlets, covering 30-day validity plans, date-to-date same-month renewal packs and standalone voice-and-SMS-only special tariff vouchers, with compliance reports due within 30 days
trends.subtitle: TRAI direction under Section 13 of the TRAI Act, 1997 · reported by Business Today, 1 October 2026
bullets: There is a category of recharge the regulator requires operators to sell and operators would rather you never found: 30-day validity plans rather than 28-day ones, date-to-date renewals inside the same month, and standalone voice-and-SMS vouchers with no data attached. They exist. They are three taps deep behind the ₹999 unlimited bundles.

TRAI's direction, issued under Section 13 of the TRAI Act, says they now get a dedicated section called "TRAI-Mandated Packs" and that section must be the first tab on the prepaid recharge screen — in the app, on the website, and at exclusive retail points of sale. Not findable. First.

The trigger is in the order's own language: TRAI says it "received various complaints from consumers regarding the lack of adequate transparency, visibility and ease of access to the different types of TRAI-mandated vouchers". Which is a regulator confirming that mandating a product and mandating that anyone can find it are two different jobs.

Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea and BSNL have 30 days from issuance — so by around 30 October — to file compliance reports. The reported beneficiary is over 200 million subscribers, concentrated among feature-phone users, older people and households that only want the phone to ring.

Worth noticing what this is not. It is not a price cap and it does not create a new tariff. It is pure interface regulation: the rule being enforced is where a thing sits on a screen. That is now a recognised category of consumer harm in Indian telecom, and it is a precedent that will not stay in telecom.

trends.headline: OpenAI says people copied its models' hidden reasoning out through the front door, and names who
trends.subject: OpenAI discloses a coordinated adversarial distillation campaign extracting protected chain-of-thought reasoning from 1 July 2026, spiking to 16,000 requests from 4,000 users on 24-25 July across a cluster of over 15,000 users, disrupted by 28 July, attributing a core cluster to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, developer of Kimi
trends.subtitle: OpenAI security disclosure, 30 September 2026
bullets: No system was breached. OpenAI is explicit that the operators "did not break our encryption, compromise a database, or gain direct access to stored user conversations". They manipulated ordinary model interactions until the model's protected reasoning — its internal working-out, normally withheld from the answer — came back out in a form the requester could read.

One of the techniques is worth understanding because it is so cheap: copy the encrypted reasoning blob from one conversation, then ask a model in a different conversation to decrypt and transcribe it. Independent researchers separately disclosed related cross-model and conversation-compaction attack paths, which OpenAI confirmed were real.

The timeline is specific. Activity from 1 July at low volume, then spikes on 24 and 25 July of 16,000 requests from over 4,000 users using one extraction pattern, with related prompt-pattern activity found across a cluster of more than 15,000 users, fully disrupted by 28 July. Disclosure came two months later.

The attribution is the part that will travel: OpenAI attributes "a core cluster of the activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi", while saying it is unclear whether all the operators were one actor. A frontier lab publicly naming another lab's people as the source of a scraping campaign is new.

The structural claim underneath is more interesting than the accusation. OpenAI says this "is not a vulnerability unique to OpenAI's models" and shared it through the Frontier Model Forum, and warns that "systems that support portable or replayable reasoning artifacts may face related risks". If you ship a reasoning model and let the trace cross conversations, you have shipped this bug.

trends.headline: Nobody has found an animal fossil older than 574 million years, and a paper on Friday argued that proves nothing
trends.subject: Science Advances paper by Durbin and Anderson removes the Weng'an Biota as a maximum-age calibration for animal origins, after Kheseen Biota microfossils from Mongolia proved equally well preserved yet still contained no animals; recalibrated molecular clocks push the divergence of the animal kingdom back to roughly 800-700 Ma, into the Cryogenian
trends.subtitle: Science Advances, 2 October 2026 · Orin Lole Durbin (Virginia Tech) and Ross Anderson (University of Oxford), with Anttila, Briggs and Macdonald
bullets: The oldest undisputed animal fossils are about 574 million years old, from the Ediacaran. For years one specific rock deposit has been used to argue that is close to the truth: the roughly 590-million-year-old Weng'an Biota in China preserves microscopic organisms in exquisite detail and contains no animals, so the reasoning went that if animals had existed, we would be looking at them.

This paper attacks that inference rather than the date. The team examined more than 140 samples from the Kheseen Biota in Mongolia, a deposit more than 40 million years younger than Weng'an, by scanning electron microscopy, and found microfossils just as finely preserved — spherical organisms, embryo-like structures with internal cells — and again no animals. The catch is that animals demonstrably existed by then.

Ross Anderson of Oxford states the consequence directly: "The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent — despite the fact we know at that point they existed." Exceptional preservation does not guarantee that animals show up in it, so a deposit without animals cannot be used as a ceiling.

Remove that ceiling and the molecular clock moves. Recalibrated against older constraints — rock formations in Norway, Australia and Arizona laid down between about 850 and 730 million years ago — the estimated origin of animals shifts back roughly 200 million years, to between 800 and 700 million. That overlaps the Cryogenian and its Snowball Earth glaciations, which began around 720 million years ago.

First author Orin Lole Durbin, now a palaeobiology doctoral student at Virginia Tech and an Oxford undergraduate when the work was done, is careful about what has and has not been shown: "this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago". The supporting evidence is chemical rather than skeletal — biomarkers consistent with sponges at least 650 million years ago. The argument is about what silence in the fossil record is allowed to mean.

research.title: Robots can already do 74% of America's physical tasks. They are cheaper than a person at 0.3% of them.
research.subtitle: Anthropic, 30 September 2026, by Russell Legate-Yang and Maxim Massenkoff
bullets: The method is a measurement trick worth stealing. They took O*NET — about 900 US occupations broken into some 19,000 job tasks — and used Claude to rate every physical task by how much environmental control a present-day robot would need to do it, on a four-tier scale from E0 to E3. That converts a vague question into a per-task score you can aggregate against employment data.

The capability number is high and the cost number is not. Robots can perform 74% of US physical tasks, making up 34% of working hours, and only 2% of physical tasks happen in genuinely unstructured environments. But robots are cost-competitive on just 0.3% of job tasks today, and at the historical rate of about 3% annual price decline, getting to 10% would take 40 years.

Those two numbers are the whole paper. What is holding automation back is not that machines cannot do the work; it is the price per hour. Which means the forecast depends on a cost curve, not a capabilities curve — a much more boring and much more predictable object.

Combined with LLM exposure, the two together reach all but one-fifth of US employment. The exposure is also not evenly spread: highly exposed workers are 20 percentage points less likely to be female and 55 percentage points less likely to hold a bachelor's degree than unexposed workers. The largest single occupation exposed to cost-competitive automation is packers and packagers.

The validation is what makes it more than an index. Run the same exposure measure backwards over 50 years of BLS wage and employment data and jobs more exposed to robots did see greater declines in wages and employment. The measure predicts the past, which is the minimum you should demand before believing it about the future.

research.title: Can Agents Design Libraries for Agents?
research.subtitle: arXiv:2609.36730, submitted 29 September 2026 · Gabriel Orlanski, Alex L. Zhang, Avi Trost, Vincent Sunn Chen, Frederic Sala, Aws Albarghouthi, Ludwig Schmidt — MIT, Stanford University and the University of Wisconsin-Madison
bullets: The premise is one you have probably already lived. Agents increasingly build on code other agents wrote, and they "reimplement rather than reuse, growing the codebases later agents must work in". So: can an agent write a library that other agents will actually use?

LibraryDesignBench runs it as two phases. A designer agent implements a full-featured library from a specification that says what capabilities are required and what the use cases are, but deliberately does not prescribe the design. Then three user agents from different model families write programs against it, and the library is scored on their correctness and simplicity — not on the library's own tests. 242 expert-validated problems across 15 library-design tasks in four languages.

The designers do fine. On eleven of the fifteen tasks, agent designers reproduce the abstractions of the human-written production library they are being compared against. The problem is downstream: user agents adopt agent-written and human-written libraries alike but underuse both, reimplementing capabilities the library already provides.

The failure analysis is the finding. The extra code is not written because something was missing — it is written "because agent-written libraries are rigid or hard to use, not because capabilities are missing". Completeness was never the bottleneck. Usability was.

Two fixes helped, and both are things you can do by hand today: give the designer more prescriptive, agent-first guidance about who is going to call this, and have it test its own library with subagents before shipping. Both improved downstream scores and produced simpler programs. Code and data are at github.com/SprocketLab/librarydesignbench.

wild.headline: Hidden Valley made its ranch dressing black and put it in a bottle that glows in the dark
wild.subject: Hidden Valley Spooky Ranch: Original Ranch dressing turned black with fruit juice and cocoa powder, bottled in glow-in-the-dark packaging for Halloween, the first seasonal variant the brand has ever made, $3.97 at Walmart
wild.subtitle: The Clorox Company press release, 24 September 2026
bullets: Spooky Ranch is Original Ranch with the colour taken out and a different one put in. It is black, the black comes from fruit juice and cocoa powder, there are no artificial flavours, and the brand insists the flavour profile is unchanged from the ranch people already buy.

The bottle glows in the dark. Not the label — the packaging. It is a $3.97 bottle of salad dressing engineered to be visible when someone turns the lights off at a Halloween party, which is a very specific and entirely correct reading of the occasion.

The genuinely surprising fact is in the press release's own framing: in a brand that has existed since 1954 and has made a life-size bottle costume, this is Hidden Valley's first-ever limited-edition seasonal product. Decades of ranch, and the first seasonal variant they shipped was a black one. Walmart exclusive, while supplies last.

wild.headline: Marshall sent three bands to play gigs at venues that no longer exist, in the shops that replaced them
wild.subject: Marshall's Dead Venue Sessions sends three emerging bands to perform at the physical sites of three closed US music venues now occupied by other businesses, filmed by documentary photographer Cheryl Dunn in three short episodes released through 2 October 2026
wild.subtitle: Pollstar, 18 September 2026
bullets: The idea is literal. Three legendary American venues have closed; Marshall sent a band to each address and had them play anyway, in whatever business is there now. Three six-minute films, directed by documentary photographer and filmmaker Cheryl Dunn, made with the agency Anomaly.

What is now standing where the stages were is the whole point. China Chalet in New York is a food court and arcade — Bronx Dominican punk band Planta Industrial debuted a single called "MIA" in it. Stalag 13, the Philadelphia DIY punk space, is a bodybuilding gym; Sweet Pill played "No Control" there. London Fog in Los Angeles, where The Doors first played, is a barber shop, and The Linda Lindas performed "Burning Out" in it.

Marshall's VP of brand marketing Christine Kennedy Grant put the arithmetic behind it in one line: "Hundreds of artists got their start on stages across the country that have since gone dark. While this series features three venues, it represents thousands." There is money attached rather than just footage — the company's Amplify programme routes 1% of online purchases to grassroots venues including Baby's All Right, Zebulon and Mohawk. The final episode landed on 2 October.

wild.headline: MilkUP opened a Toronto cafe that served dairy at four different times of day and ended each night with a cereal rave
wild.subject: Cafe Milk O'Clock, a MilkUP pop-up in Toronto over two September weekends, structured as breakfast, lunch, dinner and midnight-snack dairy stations with a gachapon machine, merch on a conveyor belt and a nightly Cereal & Milk Rave, entry free in exchange for a social post
wild.subtitle: Muse by Clios, 25 September 2026, written by the campaign's own executive creative director
bullets: Cafe Milk O'Clock ran two weekends in Toronto and was organised by time of day rather than by menu: pumpkin spice latte muffins for breakfast, alfredo bombs and smoky mozzarella sticks for the middle of the day, buttery chocolate chip cookies, and strawberries-and-cream dirty sodas for the midnight slot. You took a tray and built the day you wanted.

The mechanics were the design. You entered through one of two doors and your choice of door was your vote — chocolate or strawberry milk, cheddar or mozzarella — there was a gachapon machine, limited-edition merch came past on a conveyor belt, and every evening closed with a Cereal & Milk Rave that ended at 9pm. You left by tagging the brand, which was also how you paid.

It worked: over 6,000 people came through the first weekend. The write-up is by Chelsey Burnside of the agency Academy, which built it for Dairy Farmers of Ontario, and her stated rule is the useful bit — be "useful before you're loud". Which is a strange sentence to have to argue for, and explains most of the activations that empty out in an hour.

learn.title: India threw away 8 lakh units of donated blood last year by running out of time, not out of demand
learn.subject: Blood has a shelf life measured in days to weeks, which makes blood banking a forecasting problem rather than a storage one; India's reported discards rose 118% between 2023 and 2025 with expiry the largest single reason, and the fix for platelets was better bacterial testing rather than better fridges
body: Almost everything in a hospital store room can wait. Blood cannot. Red cells keep for a few weeks in a fridge; platelets — the component that stops you bleeding, and the one a dengue or cancer patient needs most urgently — keep for five days at room temperature, and only while being gently rocked back and forth the entire time. They are warm, nutrient-rich and sitting in plasma, which is a description of a blood product and also a description of an excellent place to grow bacteria. That, not the platelets themselves, is why the clock is five days.

So a blood bank is not a warehouse, it is a forecast. It has to guess how many units of which type will be needed in which hospital, three to seven days before anybody is injured. Get it wrong one way and someone waits. Get it wrong the other way and you pour it down a drain. India's own numbers, released to the Rajya Sabha in August from the e-Raktkosh portal, show what the second kind of error costs: collection rose 24% between 2023 and 2025, from 126.95 lakh units to 157.14 lakh. Discards rose 118%, from 8 lakh units to 17.43 lakh. The single largest reason, both years, was simply expiry — 5.47 lakh units in 2024 and 8.02 lakh in 2025, about 46% of everything thrown away. Maharashtra discarded the most in 2025 at 1.87 lakh units; Uttar Pradesh collected the most, 21.61 lakh units, and did not make the top ten for waste at all.

The good part is how one country bought itself two extra days, because the fix was not a better fridge. Canadian Blood Services wanted to move platelets from a five-day shelf life to seven, and since the limit was really about undetected bacteria, they changed the testing instead: they added an anaerobic culture bottle, they waited 36 hours after collection instead of 24 before sampling — giving any contamination longer to show itself — and they held each unit six hours before release so a flagged bag could be pulled. Two days of shelf life, bought with a delay and a second bottle, and their own engineer's estimate was roughly a 30% cut in wastage. Next time someone tells you a system has a hard physical limit, it is worth asking which measurement the limit is actually made of.

ideas.prompt: Ten things people would happily pay someone else to do for them
ideas.note: Altucher's drill: ten ideas against one prompt, written fast and not defended. Reddit rate-limited most of the feeds again this morning — only r/SomebodyMakeThis and r/Lightbulb came through — so two below are adapted from what people there were actually asking for, and the other eight are mine. Nothing here needs a developer.

items.text: Turn up on day one in someone's new flat and leave it liveable by evening: curtains up, wifi working, one shelf of groceries, bed made.
Sit with a parent for two hours and set up their phone properly — contacts, photos backed up, scam calls blocked — and then write down what you did on paper.
Read someone's insurance policy and tell them in four sentences what it does not cover.
Go to the government office for them. Queue, form, stamp, photocopy, done.
items.why: Half of what people wish existed is just someone absorbing a queue on their behalf.

items.text: Rebuild their presentation template once, properly, so every deck after that takes twenty minutes.
items.why: A recurring ask on r/SomebodyMakeThis this week was a PowerPoint editor where you customise the workspace instead of the slides — the wish is not software, it is that someone else sets it up.

items.text: Cook one enormous batch of something in their kitchen on a Sunday and leave the freezer full of labelled meals.
Be the person who returns things. Collect the pile by the door, handle every refund, send one message with the total.
Photograph and list the fifteen things in their house they keep meaning to sell.
Spend an afternoon making their building less annoying — fix the gate latch, label the meters, put a working torch by the stairs.
items.why: Somebody on r/Lightbulb this week wished for apartment buildings designed so you barely had to worry about anything; nobody is rebuilding the building, but almost all of it is a day's work.

items.text: Wait at home for the delivery, the plumber or the gas man, in the four-hour window nobody can afford to lose.
